common_diseases.name: Late blight
common_diseases.symptoms: Water-soaked lesions on leaves and fruit, white fungal growth
common_diseases.treatment: Apply copper-based fungicides and use resistant varieties

common_diseases.name: Early blight
common_diseases.symptoms: Target-shaped lesions on lower leaves, yellowing
common_diseases.treatment: Rotate crops, apply fungicide sprays such as chlorothalonil

common_diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
common_diseases.treatment: Use resistant cultivars and soil solarization

common_pests.name: Tomato fruit worm (Helicoverpa armigera)
common_pests.treatment: Biological control with Bacillus thuringiensis, pheromone traps

common_pests.name: Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
common_pests.treatment: Insecticidal soap, neem oil, reflective mulches

common_pests.name: Aphids (Myzus persicae)
common_pests.treatment: Introduce lady beetles, use insecticidal soap

crop_profile.summary: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is an annual fruit crop thriving in warm, humid climates with 18-30°C temperatures, 60-80% humidity, and 500-1000 mm annual rainfall. It prefers loam soils, pH 5.5-7.0, good drainage, and high nitrogen. Drip irrigation, balanced NPK (10-10-10) and organic amendments boost yields of 60-90 t/ha. Major producers include China, India, USA, Turkey, and Egypt. Key challenges are late blight, early blight, Fusarium wilt, and pests like fruit worm, whitefly, and aphids. Proper irrigation, fertilization, timely harvest, and refrigerated storage ensure high-quality marketable fruit.

recommendation.recommendation: Harvest the tomato crop now and execute a rapid, refrigerated supply chain to the highest‑price market (Tiruvarur) while diversifying sales to four additional nearby markets and securing processing contracts for any surplus.
recommendation.justification: Soil health (92) and vegetation vigor (NDVI 90) are excellent, and market prices are trending upward with the top price at Tiruvarur (₹1917). The crop is at the optimal fruit‑development stage for peak quality, and the main risks (perishability, transport cost, competition) can be mitigated by immediate cooling, refrigerated transport, and market diversification. This approach maximizes profitability while keeping yield risk low.
actions: 1. Schedule harvest within the next 5‑7 days to capture peak fruit quality and market price.
2. Immediately pre‑cool harvested tomatoes to 12‑14 °C and pack in ventilated, insulated crates.
3. Contract refrigerated trucks (30 °C → 12 °C) for direct delivery to Tiruvarur Market (≈293 km) and secondary markets (Thoothukudi, Kanchipuram, Tiruvannamalai, Kanyakumari).
4. Allocate 60 % of the load to Tiruvarur (highest price), 20 % to Thoothukudi, and 20 % split among the remaining three markets to spread risk.
5. Negotiate short‑term purchase agreements with local processing plants (paste, sauce) for any excess volume beyond fresh‑market demand.
6. Maintain drip irrigation at 20‑30 mm week⁻¹ until harvest to preserve fruit firmness and prevent water stress.
7. Apply post‑harvest fungicide (copper‑based) as a preventive measure against late blight during handling and transport.
8. Record batch weights, temperatures, and transport times for each market shipment.
recommendation.expected_outcome: Achieve maximum farmgate price by selling the majority of the crop fresh at Tiruvarur, reduce post‑harvest loss to <5 %, and secure additional revenue streams through processing contracts, resulting in high profitability despite transport distances.
